text: Why did Jesus have to die on the cross?
My favorite way to illustrate this is by a story. All right, let's see it.
Once upon a time, there was a king who is known by everyone in the kingdom [music] to be the most just and loving king who had ever lived. But then it was discovered that somebody [music] was
stealing from the king's treasury. And so, the king being a just king sent out an edict. When it's discovered who's stealing from the king's treasury, it would be 20 lashes. Theft continued 30
lashes until finally the king [music] issued a final decree. It will be a sentence of 40 lashes. Now, the problem with that was that 40 lashes was a death
sentence. The theft continued [music] until eventually it was discovered that none other than the king's daughter was the [music] one who was stealing. A question began to ripple through the

kingdom. Some thought he would forgive her, but then how would he be just? Some thought that he [music] would issue the sentence, but then how would he be loving? The king sat down and decided, you know what, the sentence [music] is
just, the punishment must fall. And in front of everybody, the king's own daughter was marched up to the podium.
And the executioner stood there and he began to raise his whip. And as soon as he did, [music] the king yelled, "Stop!" And he wrapped his body around his own
daughter. And he said, "The sentence must stand. It's just." And the king died in thestead of [music] his daughter. She went free because he took
the penalty. The reason Jesus had to die on the cross is because [music] God is just and so payment for sin has to be made. But God is love. So he made the
payment himself. So lots of problems with this analogy. To begin, this is what is known as penal substitutionary
atonement theory. The idea that what Jesus did was bear the wrath of God that
was intended for us as a substitution so that we did not have to suffer that
wrath. And this is really only a salient theory within American evangelicalism these days. And it really originates or
at least becomes salient during the reformation and particularly with the highly legalistic approaches of Calvin
and others. When we look at early Christianity and when we look in the Bible, we see a variety of different atonement models or ways to think about
the atonement that kind of harmonizes all the different metaphors and analogies and discussions that we find
in the Bible. And so the earliest atonement theories were like Christristus Victor and the ransom theory and things like that. Penal
substitutionary atonement theory was not considered particularly useful or particularly just or merciful. And when
we look in the biblical text, we don't really find the idea that Jesus died as
a substitutionary sacrifice to suffer the wrath of God in our place. I mean, you can interpret some texts that way,
but if you do, you're really overruling a bunch of other passages, and you're asserting an interpretation of the
sacrificial system of the Hebrew Bible that wasn't really there because there are no sacrifices in the Hebrew Bible
that are substitutionary or are about suffering or require the death of the
sinner. Because all of the sins that require the death of the sinner do not qualify for any kind of sacrifice. And
all of the sacrifices that are prescribed are not associated with sins
that merit death. And they're not substitutions. If they were substitutions, then you would have people who offer themselves or you could
at least in theory have people who offer themselves. That would be more ideal. I'm not going to offer the substitute.
I'm going to do it myself. But spilling human blood on an altar defiled the altar. So obviously these sacrifices
were not substitutions for the life of the sinner. And they also were not about suffering. The animal had to be killed
in a quick and a humane way. It was not about causing the animal to suffer. In fact, giving the animal wounds or
injuries causing it to suffer prior to the actual sacrifice itself invalidated the animal, made it no longer eligible
for use as a sacrifice. Also, the spilling of blood has an entirely different and and very complex kind of
uh conceptual framework going on in the Hebrew Bible. Jacob Mgrim has the best work on this, particularly in his Anchor
Yale Bible commentary volumes on Leviticus. But the idea was that the blood acted as kind of a metaphysical detergent to clean the metaphysical
stains of certain kinds of sin from the holy space and then from the people themselves. And again, it's not
substitutionary. It's not about suffering. It's not in place of something that would require the death
of the sinner. So, penal substitutionary atonement theory is not widely accepted by scholars who really care what the
Hebrew Bible has to say. It's mostly promoted again by American evangelicals.
And it requires not only that you endorse bad interpretations of what's going on in the Hebrew Bible, but also in the New Testament. and also that you
presuppose univocality and center and give priority to your bad interpretations of these passages from the Hebrew Bible and from the New
Testament and then use them to overrule all of the other atonement models that are presented. It silences all of the
other models. But also the little parable that is being shared by Josh is problematic in a number of ways. To
begin, it is endorsing a concept of retributive justice that if somebody does wrong, you hurt them to the degree
you believe is equivalent to the wrongdoing that they have done. Now, that's a pretty bad understanding of
justice that is already rejected in the Hebrew Bible itself, but also in the New Testament. So why are we dredging back
up a sense of justice that has already been overruled by God in the Hebrew Bible and then in the New Testament?
Again, the Bible is not univocal. So you do have retributive justice in places and you have non-retributive justice in
other places. Justice should be more restorative, reparative than it should be retributive. at least in the opinion
of it seems to me the majority of moral philosophers today. But you also have the changing punishments. We're
increasing, we're ratcheting up the punishment until it reaches the death penalty. The death penalty for stealing is not just.
Now once we move past that then we have the problem that really what the king is trying to do is appear just not be just
because where is the pressure coming from? It's coming from the perception on the part of the king's people that the king is just. So he's not actually
trying to be just for the sake of justice. He's trying to be just so that he can signal to his people that he is
just. He wants to appear just and that's why he appears just by performing the
sentence because the sentence actually includes the recipients of the
punishment. It's not the sentence if it's done to somebody else. It's just performing the sentence, but it does not
have the desired effect in order for the retributive justice to be achieved.
Again, we are just presupposing that a sentence is transferable and that
serves justice. But that doesn't punish the wrongdoer. It just punishes an innocent person.
And voluntariness is widely agreed by a lot of people to not really be an adequate gap filler for that distance
between the performance of a sentence and the actual fulfillment of the purpose of the sentence, the actual
fulfillment of justice. So the king is just performing the sentence so that his
people will perceive him to be just. And we've got another problem which I think
is best illustrated by James 2:13 where the inspired author ostensibly says that mercy triumphs over judgment.
So the idea that both must be maintained, judgment and mercy both must
be maintained by this notion of proxy punishment. Uh that's actually rejected
in the New Testament. So, this little allegory doesn't really put on display a particularly competent or thoughtful
understanding of justice or why Jesus had to die. In my opinion, if we're asking why did Jesus have to die, we're
asking the wrong question. Jesus died, we then created the story based on the fact. So, we're bringing together some
things that were initially unrelated and trying to weave them together in a way that makes them related. And that's why
you have a bunch of different ways to understand the significance of Jesus's death and how that contributes to the
salvation of humanity. Now, maybe there's a way that is coherent to tie all of them together. If so, great. That
is a wonderful piece of systematic theology. But I would point out that these are all just different ways to try to tie together things that were
ultimately unrelated. The fact that this person who went around preaching the need for forgiveness and all this was
executed by the state and then the later developed ideas about the significance of this death to the salvation of
Jesus's people. They're trying to create this connection and different people are going to create it in different ways.
And I don't really see a need to try to harmonize all the different ways to create them. I think we can just observe that Jesus died, then people came up
with ways to explain why Jesus died. And I think that's the best answer myself.
Obviously, if you're coming at this from a devotional or a confessional perspective, you're going to want a different answer, and that's fine. But I
don't think a helpful answer is penal substitutionary atonement theory. I think it's actually pretty harmful. It's
